positions/papal-infallibility/oneLine: The bishop of Rome, as successor of Peter, has full, supreme and universal jurisdiction over the Church, and when he defines ex cathedra a doctrine of faith or morals to be held by the whole Church he is preserved from error by the Holy Spirit.
positions/papal-infallibility/coreClaims: Christ made Peter the rock and gave him the keys (Matthew 16:18–19), commanded him to strengthen his brethren (Luke 22:32) and feed his sheep (John 21:15–17).
Peter's primacy continues in the bishops of Rome.
The pope has ordinary, immediate jurisdiction over all churches and pastors (Pastor Aeternus, ch. 3).
Ex cathedra definitions are irreformable ‘of themselves, and not from the consent of the Church’ (ch. 4).
Infallibility is a negative protection, not inspiration or impeccability; it has been formally invoked rarely (e.g. 1854, 1950).
positions/papal-infallibility/origin: Roman primacy appears early (Clement's letter to Corinth c. 96; Irenaeus c. 180; Pope Stephen and Cyprian, 250s); developed by Leo I (‘Peter has spoken through Leo’, 451), Gregory VII (Dictatus papae, 1075) and Boniface VIII (Unam Sanctam, 1302); infallibility discussed by Peter Olivi (c. 1280) and defined at the First Vatican Council (18 July 1870) under Pius IX; set in collegial context by Vatican II (Lumen Gentium, 1964).
positions/papal-infallibility/strongestA: The Petrine texts give Peter a unique role; the early Church recognised Rome's pre-eminence as the church of Peter and Paul (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.3.2).
A visible church needs a visible principle of unity and a final court of appeal.
Rome's doctrinal record in the early controversies (Leo's Tome, opposition to monothelitism under Martin I) was remarkably consistent.
Infallibility is limited in scope and invoked rarely, protecting the Church's unity without making the pope an oracle.
positions/papal-infallibility/strongestO: Orthodox: Peter's primacy was among equals and did not pass uniquely to Rome; the ecumenical councils, not the pope, settled doctrine (canon 28 of Chalcedon grounded Rome's status in its imperial rank).
Historical cases such as Pope Honorius I, condemned by Constantinople III (681), suggest popes erred in doctrine.
Protestants: Matthew 16 refers to Peter's confession or to Peter as an apostle among others; no successor is mentioned.
Döllinger and the Old Catholics argued it was a historical novelty unknown to the first millennium.
positions/papal-infallibility/responses/: Catholic historians answer that Honorius wrote as a private theologian, not ex cathedra.
Development of doctrine (Newman) explains how a primacy present in seed became explicit.
Vatican II and John Paul II's Ut Unum Sint (1995) invited other churches to discuss how the primacy might be exercised.
positions/papal-infallibility/consequenc: Old Catholic schism (Utrecht Union, 1889) and the Kulturkampf in Germany.
Strengthened centralisation of the Catholic Church (ultramontanism) in the 19th–20th centuries.
A central topic of Catholic–Orthodox dialogue (Ravenna Document, 2007) and of Anglican–Catholic dialogue (ARCIC, The Gift of Authority, 1999).
positions/conciliarism/oneLine: Supreme authority in the Church resides in a general council representing the whole Church, to which even the pope is subject in matters of faith, schism and reform.
positions/conciliarism/coreClaims/0: The Church as a whole, not one bishop, is indefectible.
positions/conciliarism/coreClaims/1: A general council receives its power directly from Christ and can judge and depose a pope (Haec Sancta, Constance, 1415).
positions/conciliarism/coreClaims/3: (Gallicanism, 1682) papal definitions are not irreformable without the consent of the Church.
positions/conciliarism/origin: Developed from canon lawyers' discussions of a heretical pope, by Marsilius of Padua, William of Ockham, Jean Gerson and Pierre d'Ailly, during the Western Schism (1378–1417); applied at the Council of Constance (1414–18), which deposed rival popes; weakened after the Council of Basel; condemned by Pius II (Execrabilis, 1460) and decisively by Vatican I (1870).
positions/conciliarism/strongestArgument: It ended the Western Schism when three rival popes claimed office.
The Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15) decided collectively; Paul rebuked Peter (Galatians 2:11).
It corresponds to the conciliar practice of the first millennium.
positions/conciliarism/strongestObjectio: Papalists argue that councils have no authority without the pope's confirmation.
Conciliar assemblies (Basel) proved divisive and unworkable.
Vatican I defined that papal definitions are irreformable of themselves, excluding conciliarism.
positions/conciliarism/responses/0: Conciliarists point out that the legitimacy of every later pope rests on Constance's action.
positions/conciliarism/responses/1: Vatican II's doctrine of collegiality partially rehabilitated conciliar concerns.
positions/conciliarism/consequences/1: Influenced Gallicanism, Old Catholicism and Anglican and Protestant theories of church governance.
positions/conciliarism/consequences/2: Its defeat prepared the way for papal centralisation.
positions/inerrancy/oneLine: Because Scripture is breathed out by God, it is without error in all that it affirms — including history and science — in the original manuscripts (autographs).
positions/inerrancy/coreClaims/0: Inspiration is plenary (all of Scripture) and verbal (extends to the words), working through human authors' personalities.
positions/inerrancy/coreClaims/1: God cannot lie; therefore Scripture, as his Word, is wholly true in all it affirms.
positions/inerrancy/coreClaims/2: Inerrancy applies strictly to the autographs; copies and translations are reliable to the extent they reflect them.
positions/inerrancy/coreClaims/3: Apparent errors are due to copying, misinterpretation or incomplete knowledge, and do not count against inerrancy.
positions/inerrancy/coreClaims/4: Denying inerrancy leads to a loss of biblical authority (the ‘slippery slope’).
positions/inerrancy/origin: Building on patristic, medieval and Reformation teaching on Scripture's truthfulness, formulated with precision by the Princeton theologians A. A. Hodge and B. B. Warfield (‘Inspiration’, 1881), defended in The Fundamentals (1910–15), and codified by the International Council on Biblical Inerrancy's Chicago Statement (1978).
positions/inerrancy/proponentsOther/4: Harold Lindsell (The Battle for the Bible, 1976)
positions/inerrancy/proponentsOther/5: Southern Baptist Convention (Baptist Faith and Message 2000)
positions/inerrancy/strongestArguments/0: Jesus treated Scripture as wholly authoritative: ‘the scripture cannot be broken’ (John 10:35); ‘not one jot or tittle’ (Matthew 5:18).
positions/inerrancy/strongestArguments/1: Augustine, Aquinas, Luther and Calvin all affirmed that Scripture does not err.
positions/inerrancy/strongestArguments/2: Without inerrancy, the reader decides which parts are true, making human judgement the final authority.
positions/inerrancy/strongestArguments/3: Much apparent conflict has been resolved by archaeology and better textual knowledge.
positions/inerrancy/strongestObjections/: The autographs no longer exist, making the claim unfalsifiable and practically irrelevant.
The texts show phenomena (differing numbers in Kings and Chronicles, Gospel discrepancies) that require strained harmonisation.
It imposes modern standards of scientific and historical precision on ancient literature.
Critics argue it is a 19th-century reaction to modernism, more precise than earlier tradition.
positions/inerrancy/responses/0: Inerrantists answer that the autographs are recoverable with high confidence through textual criticism.
positions/inerrancy/responses/1: The Chicago Statement allows for ancient conventions — round numbers, phenomenological language, topical arrangement — so inerrancy is not modern precision.
positions/inerrancy/responses/2: Historians such as John Woodbridge argue that the essence of inerrancy is ancient, not a Princeton invention.
positions/inerrancy/consequences/0: Defining issue of North American fundamentalist–modernist conflicts and later evangelical boundary disputes.
positions/inerrancy/consequences/1: The Southern Baptist Convention's ‘conservative resurgence’ (1979–90s) and the founding of new seminaries.
positions/inerrancy/consequences/2: Widely held in global evangelical and Pentecostal churches; in tension with young-earth vs old-earth debates.
positions/limited-inerrancy/oneLine: Scripture is fully reliable and authoritative — infallible — in what it intends to teach about God, salvation, faith and life, but need not be free of every incidental error in matters of science, chronology or detail.
positions/limited-inerrancy/coreClaims/0: The purpose of Scripture is to make us ‘wise unto salvation’ (2 Timothy 3:15).
positions/limited-inerrancy/coreClaims/1: Inspiration works through human authors with the knowledge of their time.
positions/limited-inerrancy/coreClaims/2: Authority lies in Scripture's divinely intended message, not its incidental details.
positions/limited-inerrancy/coreClaims/3: This view allows honest engagement with critical scholarship without loss of faith.
positions/limited-inerrancy/origin: Precedents in Augustine's and Calvin's doctrine of accommodation; held by British evangelicals such as James Orr; became prominent at Fuller Theological Seminary, which revised its statement of faith (1971–72); Lausanne Covenant (1974) affirmed Scripture ‘without error in all that it affirms’, a phrase read in both ways. Catholic Dei Verbum 11 speaks of truth ‘for the sake of salvation’.
positions/limited-inerrancy/proponentsOt: Jack Rogers & Donald McKim (The Authority and Interpretation of the Bible, 1979)
positions/limited-inerrancy/strongestArg: It matches Scripture's stated purpose: salvation and godliness.
It takes the human, historical character of the Bible seriously.
It avoids staking faith on harmonising every detail.
Dei Verbum 11's wording points in a similar direction for Catholics.
positions/limited-inerrancy/strongestObj: Inerrantists: if Scripture errs in history, why trust it about the resurrection, which is a historical claim?
It is hard to separate ‘salvific’ from ‘incidental’ content consistently.
Warfield and the Chicago Statement argue that Scripture claims truthfulness in all its parts.
positions/limited-inerrancy/responses/0: Proponents answer that genre and authorial intent guide what a text affirms; the resurrection is central to the gospel's intent, unlike, say, numbers in Chronicles.
positions/limited-inerrancy/responses/1: They argue the inerrancy–infallibility distinction mirrors the Bible's own unconcern with modern precision.
positions/limited-inerrancy/consequences: The ‘Battle for the Bible’ in North American evangelicalism (1970s).
Broadened evangelical engagement with biblical criticism in Britain and elsewhere.
positions/historical-critical-method/one: The Bible should be studied like other ancient literature, with historical and literary methods, to reconstruct its sources, authors, dates and settings — whatever the theological implications.
positions/historical-critical-method/cor: Biblical books have complex histories of composition and editing (e.g. the J, E, D and P sources of the Pentateuch).
Texts must be read in their original historical context before theological application.
Traditional authorship claims (e.g. Moses, Isaiah 40–66, the Pastorals) are open to historical judgement.
Supernatural claims are assessed with historical methods (in many practitioners, under methodological naturalism).
positions/historical-critical-method/ori: Anticipated by Spinoza (1670) and Richard Simon (1678); developed in German universities by J. S. Semler, J. G. Eichhorn, W. M. L. de Wette, D. F. Strauss (Life of Jesus, 1835), F. C. Baur and Julius Wellhausen (Prolegomena, 1878); entered British debate with Essays and Reviews (1860) and William Robertson Smith's trial (1881).
positions/historical-critical-method/str: It takes seriously that God's Word came through real human history and languages.
It explains features of the texts (doublets, differing names for God, Synoptic parallels) better than traditional authorship assumptions.
Its tools have greatly advanced understanding of ancient contexts, languages and textual history.
Catholic teaching (Divino Afflante Spiritu, 1943; Dei Verbum, 1965) endorses its responsible use.
When joined to methodological naturalism, it excludes divine action in advance, prejudging miracles and prophecy.
Its hypotheses shift and sometimes reflect the scholar's own assumptions (e.g. Wellhausen's evolutionary view of religion).
It can fragment the text, losing its canonical unity and theological message.
Conservative critics argue it contributed to declining confidence in Scripture in Western churches.
positions/historical-critical-method/res: Practitioners distinguish the method from naturalistic presuppositions; many believing scholars use it.
Canonical criticism (Brevard Childs) and theological interpretation seek to integrate critical findings with the final form of the text.
positions/historical-critical-method/con: The modernist–fundamentalist controversy and heresy trials (Robertson Smith 1881, Briggs 1893).
Catholic Modernist crisis (Pascendi, 1907) followed by gradual acceptance (1943, 1965).
Standard method in university biblical studies worldwide.
